name: Sorghum

project_scope.source_pool: Master Plant Pool rows 1110–1111; Genus Study Index row 149
project_scope.learner_status: comparison/reference genus text only. Neither species is installed in data/manifest.json and this lane does not approve or install them.
project_scope.native_range_guardrail: Both are introduced grasses in Central Texas; they are not counted among confirmed native target-zone taxa. S. bicolor includes cultivated grain/forage forms and escaped shattercane; S. halepense is invasive Johnsongrass.

shared_genus_recognition.look_here_first: Find a true grass node and collar/ligule, then trace one flowering branch to paired spikelets: a larger usually bisexual SESSILE spikelet attached directly to the short axis and a PEDICELLATE companion spikelet on a stalk, often staminate or sterile. This separates Sorghum from lookalike panicle grasses far more reliably than its white leaf midrib alone.
shared_traits: Tall warm-season grasses with broad leaves and prominent midribs, jointed culms, terminal branched panicles and paired spikelets at the end of small racemes.
The fertile sessile spikelet bears a caryopsis enclosed by hardened glumes; the partner pedicellate spikelet may be staminate or functionally sterile.
Panicle shape changes with domestication: broad compact sorghum grain head is common but feral/crop lines can have lax heads; don't mistake cultivar form for a separate species.

terminology.definition: Membrane/hairy boundary on inner collar where leaf blade meets sheath.
Belowground horizontal stem with scale leaves and nodes; Johnsongrass can regenerate from its rhizomes.
Branched flower/seed head; Sorghum has short raceme units at branch tips.
Spikelet directly attached without a stalk, typically fruit-producing in these Sorghum species.
Companion spikelet on a small stalk; may be male or sterile.
Ripe spikelets naturally detach/disarticulate from panicle; wild Johnsongrass shatters much more readily than selected grain sorghum.

shared_genus_recognition.handling: Photograph rhizomes where exposed from maintenance, not by disturbing protected/native plant roots. For invasive Johnsongrass, do not scatter seed or rhizome fragments. Do not sample or feed stressed Sorghum foliage to livestock; cyanogenic glycosides can be hazardous under some conditions.

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Usually cultivated/feral ANNUAL or short-lived perennial, with fibrous roots and no extensive creeping rhizomes
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Robust PERENNIAL with extensive tough scaly rhizomes; emerges in patches from underground stems
species_comparison_matrix.weight: MOST IMPORTANT vegetative split; document exposed rhizome with nodes/scale leaves

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Very variable from dense grain heads to lax shattercane/forage panicles depending on cultivar/escape
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Usually conspicuously open, pyramidal to lanceolate panicle with spreading branches
species_comparison_matrix.weight: FIRST DISTANT CLUE, not taxonomic proof

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Typically broader blades, often 2–10 cm (20–100 mm), especially grain/forage types
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Typically narrower blades ~0.8–4 cm (8–40 mm); broad forms overlap

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Fertile sessile and companion pedicelled spikelet at branch tips; often larger, plump caryopsis in crop forms
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Fertile sessile spikelet ~3.8–6.5 mm long with companion stalked usually staminate spikelet; short spikelet-bearing branchlets

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Cultivated grain types have nonshattering or tardily shedding spikelets, but feral shattercane can readily shatter
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Rachis normally disarticulates readily below sessile spikelets, scattering ripe units

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Grain colors white, reddish, brown and many others; awns vary by cultivar and wild/feral line
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Spikelets often straw/brown/reddish-purple; lemma may be awnless or have short geniculate twisted awn (~0–13 mm)
species_comparison_matrix.weight: LOW; colors and awns cannot distinguish reliably

species_comparison_matrix.S. bicolor: Grain crop, planted forage, birdseed/roadside spill or escaped shattercane
species_comparison_matrix.S. halepense: Road edges, disturbed ditches, riparian corridors, turf edges and perennial infestations
species_comparison_matrix.weight: CONTEXT NOT PROOF: feral bicolor can occur on roadsides too

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: whole plant plus collar/ligule and a real culm node
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Confirm a grass and record mature height, blade width and white midrib only as supporting traits.

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: basal stem and naturally exposed underground stems
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Thick segmented creeping scaly rhizomes strongly indicate perennial S. halepense; no rhizomes and a fibrous annual clump lean S. bicolor.
Open large loose branched panicle leans halepense; compact densely seeded grain head leans domesticated bicolor, but feral bicolor overlaps.

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: single intact spikelet PAIR with mm scale
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Identify pedicelled versus sessile spikelet and the lower vs upper glumes, rachis attachment, awn if any; ensure true Sorghum architecture.

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: ripe head still on plant; unforced naturally detached units
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Easy seedhead shattering favors halepense but escaped S. bicolor can shatter; don't shake plants or spread seed to test.

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: no underground, flower/fruit evidence or irregular suspected hybrid
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Use Sorghum sp. or S. bicolor/halepense complex as appropriate; photo set incomplete and gene flow/feral line possible.

diagnostic_photo_requirements.show: Side view of intact underground horizontal white/tan segmented rhizome with nodes and buds on halepense; clean fibrous base on bicolor. Photograph roots already exposed by maintenance; avoid scattering fragments.
MM ruler and arrows for sessile fruiting spikelet, pedicel, pedicellate companion, glumes, awn and rachis. Use transmitted macro or dissecting microscope.
Compact domestic bicolor, lax/feral bicolor and open halepense. Three panels explicitly show overlap rather than a false binary.

diagnostic_photo_requirements.role: collar zone ligule and blade widths
diagnostic_photo_requirements.show: Ligule membrane/cilia, sheath, true node, leaf blade with cm scale and pale midrib.
Naturally retained bicolor crop grains versus disarticulated halepense mature branch, with cautious exception for shattercane.
Sorghum companion fully formed pedicellate spikelet versus Sorghastrum pedicellate partner highly reduced/vestigial; include mm macro and count structures.
Johnsongrass perennial patches alongside seeded grain/forage plants; habitat does not identify species alone.

local_lookalike_routing.name: Sorghastrum nutans (Indiangrass; desirable native)
local_lookalike_routing.separator: Sorghastrum has long awns and a highly reduced companion pedicelled spikelet (often represented by pedicel); Sorghum halepense has a formed companion spikelet. Check grass florets under magnification before deciding management.

local_lookalike_routing.name: Panicum virgatum (switchgrass; native)
local_lookalike_routing.separator: Large open panicles overlap in silhouette but Panicum spikelet architecture lacks Sorghum's characteristic sessile–pedicellate pair.

local_lookalike_routing.name: Zea mays (maize)
local_lookalike_routing.separator: Broad grass foliage with white midrib may overlap but distinct terminal staminate tassel and separate ear; not a Sorghum terminal fruiting panicle.

local_lookalike_routing.name: Sorghum almum and bicolor × halepense / feral forms
local_lookalike_routing.separator: Perennial or hybrid forage sorghums can complicate annual-versus-rhizomatous separation. Photograph underground organs and spikelet pairs; expert confirmation if traits conflict.

local_lookalike_routing.name: Setaria spp.
local_lookalike_routing.separator: Foxtail head has conspicuous bristles subtending spikelets; no Sorghum sessile/pedicellate pairing.

scientific_cautions: Neither taxon is presently canonical; this genus backfill does not install them or alter source-pool approval.
Both are introduced to Central Texas; S. bicolor is African-origin cultivated, S. halepense Eurasian/African-origin introduced invasive. This is not a native-only recommendation.
Domestic S. bicolor may be a nonrhizomatous perennial in frost-free settings, so do not equate 'can resprout' with halepense; belowground creeping rhizomes are the stronger character.
Shattercane is a feral/weedy S. bicolor form with shattering seeds and sometimes open heads. It defeats simplistic panicle and seed-retention shortcuts.
Some sorghum hybrids and forage cultivars cross or show perennial/rhizomatous traits; unresolved hybrids should not be forced into one bin.
Management relevance: removing one Johnson grass shoot is not rhizome eradication; vegetative fragment movement can spread it. This is ID guidance, not a chemical treatment prescription.
Prominent white leaf midrib occurs in multiple grasses and should never be an exclusive ID trait.
Sorghastrum nutans is a desirable native look-alike: require spikelet anatomy before labeling a restored grass invasive.

handoffs.request: Acquire rights-cleared exact-species matched photos emphasizing rhizome nodes, paired fertile/sterile spikelets and mature panicle variability. Capture field scales and photographers/licensing.

handoffs.target: Feral S. bicolor vs S. halepense and hybrid/forage taxon
handoffs.request: Confirm close identifications with FNA treatment and herbarium vouchers; use conservative tags for suspected hybrids.
